title: What to Gift Someone You Barely Know
summary: What to gift someone you barely know in Pakistan: safe sizeless gift ideas by occasion and budget band, what to avoid, and how to order in time.
body_markdown:
Buy something useful, consumable and sizeless. That is most of the answer. Dates and dry fruit, a tea or mug set, a plain stole, a mild attar, a wall clock, a bedsheet set — none of these need you to know the person's size, their taste in clothes or how their household runs, and none of them look like a guess. Decide your budget band before you start browsing rather than after. Then order early enough that the parcel lands before the event, and order it cash on delivery so you can open it and look at the thing before you pay for it.


This guide covers the gifts that are hard to get wrong, the ones worth avoiding, how to match a gift to the occasion, and how to buy online without cutting the timing fine.


## The test a safe gift has to pass


When you know someone, you buy for their taste. When you barely know them, you are buying for a stranger who will open it in front of other people, so the gift has to survive not knowing. Four questions sort almost everything:


- **Does it need a size?** If yes, put it back. Clothes, shoes and rings are the gifts most often received once and never worn.
- **Does it assume something personal?** Diet, religious practice, body, marital status, whether there are children in the house. If the gift only works when your assumption is right, it is a gamble.
- **Is it used up, or used daily?** Consumables and plain daily objects both work, because neither has to be loved forever or put on display.
- **Would it be fine if they passed it on?** A gift someone can hand to a cousin without insulting you is a kind gift. A monogrammed one cannot be passed on at all.


Anything that clears those four is a defensible choice, even if it is not exciting. For someone you barely know, unexciting and correct beats memorable and wrong.


## Gifts that are hard to get wrong


Roughly in order of how safe they are.


### Food you can hand over sealed


Dates, dry fruit, honey, a box of chocolates, a tin of decent tea. Sealed factory packaging is doing two useful things: it tells them nothing has been opened, and it lets them put the box out for guests instead of eating it alone. Dry fruit in particular reads as generous in almost every Pakistani household, and nobody has to pretend to like it.


One rule: keep homemade food for people you actually know. A stranger cannot tell whether your kitchen is clean and will not ask.


### Tea things and small kitchen items


A mug set, a steel teapot, a tray, a set of glasses, a storage jar set. Every household runs tea, and kitchen items are used by whoever is in the house rather than only by the person you handed them to — which is exactly what you want when the gift is for a family you have met once. Our guide to[kitchen gadgets worth the counter space](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/kitchen-gadgets-worth-the-counter-space) is a useful filter here: the things that get used daily make good gifts, and the single-purpose novelty gadgets do not.


### A stole, scarf or shawl


This is the one fabric gift that has no size. A plain or small-patterned stole in a neutral shade works for a colleague, a neighbour, an aunt or a teacher, and it works whether the person is tall, short, slim or not. Buy the fabric quality up and the pattern down — a plain good shawl looks considered, a loud cheap one looks like a filler gift.


### Attar or a light perfume


Scent is a good gift with one condition: keep it mild and fresh rather than heavy or distinctive. A heavy signature scent is a statement about someone's personality, and you do not know their personality. Attar is often the safer pick for an older or more traditional recipient.


Buy scent where you can inspect it on arrival, because this is the category where fakes circulate most. Our guide on[where to buy beauty and cosmetics online in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/where-to-buy-beauty-cosmetics-online-in-pakistan) covers how to read a listing and what to check on the box before you accept a parcel.


### Plain home things: a clock, bedsheets, a prayer mat


A wall clock, a good bedsheet set, a prayer mat, a set of towels. These are bought by every household eventually, which is the definition of a safe gift. Keep the colours neutral — white, cream, grey, navy — because you are not decorating their house for them.


A prayer mat is thoughtful and widely welcome, but only if you already know the household prays; if you are unsure, choose something else rather than making a statement about someone's practice.


### Something for their children


If you know there are children, a toy is the easiest gift in this whole list, because you are no longer guessing at an adult's taste. The only thing to get right is the age band, and a toy aimed slightly older than the child is usually better than one aimed younger. Our guide on[choosing toys by age without wasting money](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/choosing-toys-by-age-without-wasting-money) sets out what actually gets played with at each stage.


### Stationery: a diary, a pen, a desk set


This is the standard office answer and it deserves its reputation. A hardbound diary, a decent pen, a desk organiser or a document folder are all sizeless, useful and impossible to read as too personal — which is what makes them right for a manager, a client or a colleague you sit near but do not know well.


### A watch, if the budget is there


A watch is a step up in both cost and risk: it is a visible, personal object. Keep the dial plain and the strap neutral, and know exactly which kind of stock you are buying before you spend, because original, unbranded and copy watches sit at very different price points and a gift is the wrong place to be surprised. Our guide on[where to buy watches online in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/where-to-buy-watches-online-in-pakistan) explains how to tell them apart on a listing.


## What to leave on the shelf


- **Anything with a size.** Clothes, shoes, gloves, rings. The exceptions are the sizeless ones above: stoles, shawls, scarves.
- **Strongly scented or "statement" perfume.** Too much of a guess about a person you have met twice.
- **Very cheap electronics.** A charger or earbuds that die in a month become your gift in their memory. If you are gifting electronics, buy fewer, better items.
- **Anything needing assembly or a setup.** A gift that comes with a job attached is not a gift.
- **Religious items you are not sure about.** Well-meant and easy to get wrong across different practices.
- **Visible price stickers and the seller's invoice.** Peel the sticker, take the slip out, and never forward an online parcel to the recipient unopened.
- **Anything second-hand or in opened packaging.** Fine between friends, awkward with a stranger.
- **Cash in an envelope where a gift is expected.** At some events cash is the norm; at an office farewell or a first visit to someone's home, it lands as a shortcut.


## Set the band before you browse


The mistake is browsing first and letting the nicest thing you happen to see set the budget. Decide the band, then shop inside it. Three bands cover almost every situation:


- **A token.** A colleague's last day, a neighbour's new baby, a thank-you. Sweets, dry fruit, a mug, a diary, a small plant.
- **A proper gift.** A wedding you were invited to by association, an in-laws' first visit, a boss's farewell. A shawl, a tea set, bedsheets, a clock, a gift hamper.
- **Something significant.** A close colleague's wedding, a family event you are representing your household at. A watch, a large home item, a multi-piece set.


What fits in each band moves with the season and the seller, so set your band, then sort by price rather than browsing by hope. Occasion clusters — Eid, wedding season, back to school — are when the same gift categories are in heaviest demand, and it is worth checking the[Markaz deals page](https://www.markaz.app/shop/deals) before you commit at the top of your band.


## Matching the gift to the occasion


- **An office colleague leaving.** Stationery, a mug or tumbler, a desk plant, sweets for the floor. Keep it neutral enough that everyone can sign the card.
- **A boss or a client.** Dry fruit, a dates box, a diary set, tea. Nothing wearable, nothing personal, nothing that jokes.
- **A wedding you were invited to by association.** Home items are the point of a wedding gift: bedsheets, a dinner set, glassware, a clock. Our[Pakistani wedding shopping checklist](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/the-pakistani-wedding-shopping-checklist-and-when-to-buy-each-thing) covers the timing side, which matters if the invitation came late.
- **Eid.** Sweets, dry fruit, attar, a stole, something for the children of the house. Hampers work because one gift covers a whole family.
- **A new baby.** Bedding, towels, a blanket, or a gift for the mother rather than the baby. Skip newborn clothes — everyone else is buying those, and sizes run out fast.
- **A new home.** Anything for the kitchen or the drawing room, plus a plant. A housewarming gift can be plain and still land.
- **A neighbour or your child's teacher.** Food, sealed, handed over at the door. This is the right place for the token band.


## Presentation does more work than price


Two minutes of wrapping changes how the same object reads. Wrap it or put it in a bag, write two lines on a card by hand, and remove every trace of what you paid. If the gift is food, a tray or a basket instead of the plastic bag it arrived in is the whole upgrade.


Write the card before the day. The line you improvise at the door is always worse than the one you wrote sitting down, and for someone you barely know the card is doing the work of the relationship you do not have yet.


## Buying gifts online without cutting it fine


Gifts have a deadline, which makes them different from ordinary shopping. Two habits cover it.


First, order to your own address, not the recipient's. You want to see the thing, remove the invoice, wrap it, and be able to fix it if something is wrong. Cash on delivery helps here for the same reason: local orders on Markaz are paid when the parcel reaches you, so you can open the box, check the colour and the piece count, and pay only then.


Second, work backwards from the date. Local orders move in 3–5 days across Pakistan. Ordering factory-direct through[Markaz China](https://www.markaz.app/china) takes 10–17 days and is the cheaper route, so it works for a wedding you have known about for a month and not for a farewell on Friday. For anything urgent, buy local and accept the price.


A few listing checks save most of the disappointments:


- **Count the pieces.** A "tea set" can be two cups or twelve. The number is in the listing, not in the photo.
- **Read the measurements, not the adjectives.** "Large" tray tells you nothing; centimetres do.
- **Check the material line** for anything steel, glass or fabric.
- **Look at the return window** before you order something you cannot re-gift.

For gifts the browsing shortcut is usually the category listing: the[Markaz product categories](https://www.markaz.app/shop/categories) put the home, kitchen, fashion-accessory and kids' sections side by side, which is roughly how gift decisions are actually made.


## When you have to gift several people at once


An office floor, a set of Eid hampers, the four households you visit every year. Buying one thing for everyone is not lazy here — it is the only way it stays fair, and nobody compares hampers.


Pick one item, order a single unit first, look at it, then order the rest. There is no minimum order quantity on Markaz, so the test unit costs you nothing extra and it is the cheapest way to avoid twenty identical mistakes. If you are buying at any volume, browsing the[Markaz supplier list](https://www.markaz.app/shop/supplier/list) is the quickest way to see who actually stocks depth in one category, which matters when you need the same item twenty times rather than once.

## Frequently asked questions


**What is the safest gift for someone I have met once?** Sealed food — dates, dry fruit or good chocolates — handed over in a bag or a tray. It needs no size, assumes nothing about them, can be shared with whoever is in the house, and nobody has to pretend.


**Is it rude to give a gift that is obviously inexpensive?** No. Wrapped, presented and handed over with a line on a card, a token gift reads as thoughtful. Unwrapped, with the price sticker still on it, even an expensive gift reads badly. Presentation carries more than the amount.


**Can I give clothes if I know their size?** If you actually know it, yes, but the risk is still taste rather than fit. A stole, a shawl or a scarf gets you the fabric gift without either problem.


**How far ahead should I order a gift online?** For a local order, allow the 3–5 day delivery window plus a day to wrap. For a China-direct order, the window is 10–17 days, so it only works when the date is at least three weeks out.


**Can I order a gift with cash on delivery?** Yes, and it is the better way to do it. Local orders on Markaz are cash on delivery, so the parcel reaches you first and you pay after checking the colour, the piece count and the packaging — the three things a photo will not settle.


**What should I buy for a whole family I barely know?** One hamper for the household rather than individual gifts: dry fruit or sweets, plus a home item like a tray or a tea set. It covers everyone, avoids ranking people, and nobody is left out.


**Are gift cards acceptable in Pakistan?** Between friends and for younger recipients, often yes. For a first gift to a colleague, a senior or someone's parents, a physical gift still lands better — a card asks them to do the shopping you were supposed to do.
